claim: Biological wastewater treatment plants (BWWTP) are considered to be hotspots for the evolution and subsequent spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
source: Biological wastewater treatment plants (BWWTP) are considered to be hotspots for the evolution and subsequent spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
evidence: This is a statement presented in the abstract without specific data from this study, but is supported by the general context and citations in the introduction.

claim: Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) promote the mobilization and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs).
source: Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) promote the mobilization and dissemination of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) and are thereby critical mediators of AMR within the BWWTP microbial community.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: A core group of 15 AMR categories were found across all timepoints in the BWWTP.
source: Our results showed a core group of 15 AMR categories which were found across all timepoints.
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal metagenomic data analysis presented in Figure 1b.

claim: Bacitracin resistance was disseminated exclusively via plasmids.
source: Some of these AMR categories were disseminated exclusively (bacitracin) or primarily (aminoglycoside, MLS and sulfonamide) via plasmids or phages (fosfomycin and peptide)
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic data comparing ARG localization on plasmids versus phages, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Aminoglycoside, MLS and sulfonamide resistance were disseminated primarily via plasmids.
source: Some of these AMR categories were disseminated exclusively (bacitracin) or primarily (aminoglycoside, MLS and sulfonamide) via plasmids or phages (fosfomycin and peptide)
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic data comparing ARG localization on plasmids versus phages, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Fosfomycin and peptide resistance were disseminated via phages.
source: Some of these AMR categories were disseminated exclusively (bacitracin) or primarily (aminoglycoside, MLS and sulfonamide) via plasmids or phages (fosfomycin and peptide)
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic data comparing ARG localization on plasmids versus phages, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Aminoglycoside, bacitracin and sulfonamide resistance genes were expressed more by plasmids.
source: Combined and timepoint-specific analyses of gene, transcript and protein abundances further demonstrated that aminoglycoside, bacitracin and sulfonamide resistance genes were expressed more by plasmids, in contrast to fosfomycin and peptide AMR expression by phages, thereby validating our genomic findings.
evidence: This is supported by metatranscriptomic data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Fosfomycin and peptide AMR were expressed by phages.
source: Combined and timepoint-specific analyses of gene, transcript and protein abundances further demonstrated that aminoglycoside, bacitracin and sulfonamide resistance genes were expressed more by plasmids, in contrast to fosfomycin and peptide AMR expression by phages, thereby validating our genomic findings.
evidence: This is supported by metatranscriptomic data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Candidatus Microthrix parvicella was a major contributor to several AMR categories in the analyzed communities.
source: In the analyzed communities, the dominant taxon Candidatus Microthrix parvicella was a major contributor to several AMR categories whereby its plasmids primarily mediated aminoglycoside resistance.
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic linkage of ARGs shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Candidatus Microthrix parvicella plasmids primarily mediated aminoglycoside resistance.
source: In the analyzed communities, the dominant taxon Candidatus Microthrix parvicella was a major contributor to several AMR categories whereby its plasmids primarily mediated aminoglycoside resistance.
evidence: This is supported by MGE-specific taxonomic linkage shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and Figure 6b.

claim: AMR associated with ESKAPEE pathogens was found within the BWWTP.
source: Importantly, we also found AMR associated with ESKAPEE pathogens within the BWWTP, and here MGEs also contributed differentially to the dissemination of the corresponding ARGs.
evidence: This is supported by pathogen-specific AMR analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: MGEs contributed differentially to the dissemination of ARGs in ESKAPEE pathogens.
source: Importantly, we also found AMR associated with ESKAPEE pathogens within the BWWTP, and here MGEs also contributed differentially to the dissemination of the corresponding ARGs.
evidence: This is supported by pathogen-specific MGE analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The use of antibiotics has exacerbated the emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in both commensal and pathogenic bacteria.
source: However, the use of antibiotics has exacerbated the emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in both commensal and pathogenic bacteria (Wright, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wright, 2007.

claim: AMR has become a prevalent threat to human health.
source: As a result, AMR, as the 'silent pandemic', has become a prevalent threat to human health (Brogan and Mossialos, 2016; Mahoney et al., 2021; O'Neill, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brogan and Mossialos, 2016; Mahoney et al., 2021; O'Neill, 2014.

claim: BWWTPs are considered hotspots of AMR due to the convergence of antibiotics with resistant, potentially pathogenic microorganisms.
source: From a public health perspective, biological wastewater treatment plants (BWWTPs) are considered hotspots of AMR due to the convergence of antibiotics with resistant, potentially pathogenic microorganisms originating from both the general population as well as agriculture, healthcare services and industry (Alexander et al., 2020; Rodríguez-Molina et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alexander et al., 2020; Rodríguez-Molina et al., 2019.

claim: The mobilization of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) through horizontal gene transfer (HGT) promotes the dissemination of AMR within the BWWTP microbial community.
source: Additionally, the mobilization of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) through rampant horizontal gene transfer (HGT) promotes the dissemination of AMR within the BWWTP microbial community (von Wintersdorff et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to von Wintersdorff et al., 2016.

claim: BWWTPs represent an environment exceptionally suited for the evolution and subsequent spread of AMR.
source: Therefore, BWWTPs represent an environment exceptionally suited for the evolution and subsequent spread of AMR (Calero-Cáceres et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Calero-Cáceres et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013.

claim: More than 32 studies have documented the role of BWWTPs as key reservoirs of AMR.
source: To date, more than 32 studies have documented the role of BWWTPs as key reservoirs of AMR (Fouz et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fouz et al., 2020.

claim: BWWTPs generally do not contain the necessary infrastructure to remove either ARGs or resistant bacteria.
source: Furthermore, BWWTPs generally do not contain the necessary infrastructure to remove either ARGs or resistant bacteria, which are released into the receiving water via the effluent, promoting its spread in the environment at large (Alexander et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Alexander et al., 2020.

claim: ARGs and resistant bacteria are released into receiving water via the effluent, promoting spread in the environment.
source: Furthermore, BWWTPs generally do not contain the necessary infrastructure to remove either ARGs or resistant bacteria, which are released into the receiving water via the effluent, promoting its spread in the environment at large (Alexander et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Alexander et al., 2020.

claim: Surface water bodies such as rivers contribute to the further dissemination of AMR and resistant bacteria among environmental microorganisms.
source: Most often these are surface water bodies such as rivers, which contribute to the further dissemination of AMR and resistant bacteria among environmental microorganisms (Singer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Singer et al., 2016.

claim: There is strong evidence suggesting that ARGs from environmental bacteria can be taken up by human-associated and pathogenic bacteria.
source: In fact, there is strong evidence suggesting that ARGs from environmental bacteria can be taken up by human-associated and pathogenic bacteria (Nadeem et al., 2020; Trinh et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nadeem et al., 2020; Trinh et al., 2018.

claim: BWWTPs provide samples representative of entire populations from an epidemiological and surveillance perspective.
source: From an epidemiological and surveillance perspective, BWWTPs also provide samples representative of entire populations (Hendriksen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hendriksen et al., 2019.

claim: BWWTPs have been crucial for the monitoring of SARS-CoV-2 within the human population.
source: As such, BWWTPs have recently been crucial for the monitoring of SARS-CoV-2 within the human population (Herold et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Herold et al., 2021.

claim: Antibiotic selection pressures may alter HGT processes, thereby increasing the number of resistance elements which reside on mobile DNA.
source: Previous work has in particular shown that antibiotic selection pressures may alter HGT processes, thereby increasing the number of resistance elements which reside on mobile DNA (Datta and Hughes, 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Datta and Hughes, 1983.

claim: Acquisition of ARGs via MGEs primarily occurs through two mechanisms: conjugation or transduction.
source: Acquisition of ARGs via MGEs primarily occurs through two mechanisms: conjugation or transduction (MacLean and San Millan, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to MacLean and San Millan, 2019.

claim: In conjugation, plasmids carrying one or more resistance genes are transferred between microorganisms.
source: In conjugation, plasmids carrying one or more resistance genes are transferred between microorganisms (Carattoli, 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Carattoli, 2013.

claim: In transduction, bacteriophages carrying ARGs infect bacteria and integrate their genome into those of the host thereby conferring resistance.
source: while in transduction bacteriophages carrying ARGs infect bacteria and integrate their genome into those of the host thereby conferring resistance (Chiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chiang et al., 2019.

claim: Conjugation is often thought to have the greatest influence on the dissemination of ARGs, while transduction is deemed less important.
source: Of these mechanisms, conjugation is often thought to have the greatest influence on the dissemination of ARGs, while transduction is deemed less important (von Wintersdorff et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to von Wintersdorff et al., 2016.

claim: The contributions of plasmids and phages as independent entities to AMR transmission within complex communities is largely unknown.
source: This circumstance has created a knowledge gap whereby the contributions of plasmids and phages as independent entities to AMR transmission within complex communities, such as those found in biological BWWTPs, is largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: 29 different categories of AMR were found within the BWWTP.
source: This analysis revealed the presence of 29 different categories of AMR within the BWWTP.
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis using the PathoFact pipeline.

claim: Longitudinal analyses highlighted enrichments in aminoglycoside, beta-lactam and multidrug resistance genes.
source: Subsequent longitudinal analyses highlighted enrichments in aminoglycoside, beta-lactam and multidrug resistance genes (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal metagenomic data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: A transient change at two timepoints (13-05-2011, 08-02-2012) highlighted a steep increase in resistance genes corresponding to glycopeptide resistance.
source: For example, a transient change at two timepoints (13-05-2011, 08-02-2012) highlighted a steep increase in resistance genes corresponding to glycopeptide resistance.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal metagenomic data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Six AMR categories (aminocoumarin, aminoglycoside:aminocoumarin, elfamycin, nucleoside, triclosan, and unclassified) were found to be prevalent (>75% of all timepoints).
source: A further six (aminocoumarin, aminoglycoside:aminocoumarin, elfamycin, nucleoside, triclosan, and unclassified) AMR categories were found to be prevalent (>75% of all timepoints)
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal presence/absence analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Three AMR categories were moderately (50–75% of all timepoints) present over time.
source: while another three AMR categories were moderately (50–75% of all timepoints) present over time (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal presence/absence analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Five AMR categories were rarely present within the BWWTP, with resistance corresponding to acridine dye only present at six of the timepoints.
source: Five other categories were rarely present within the BWWTP, with resistance corresponding to acridine dye only present at six of the timepoints.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal presence/absence analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Aminoglycoside, beta-lactam, and multidrug resistance identified at high levels in metagenomic information were also highly expressed within the BWWTP.
source: Aminoglycoside, beta-lactam, and multidrug resistance identified at high levels in metagenomic information were also highly expressed within the BWWTP (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by metatranscriptomic data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Peptide resistance demonstrated the highest expression levels of all the AMR categories.
source: However, peptide resistance demonstrated the highest expression levels of all the AMR categories.
evidence: This is supported by metatranscriptomic data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: ~90% of the expressed peptide resistance was directly contributed by a single resistance gene, YojI.
source: We further investigated which ARG subtypes contributed to the identified peptide resistance category and found that ~90% of the expressed peptide resistance was directly contributed by a single resistance gene, YojI, which was found to be widely distributed among the major taxa comprising the BWWTP community such as the Comamonadaceae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by detailed analysis of peptide resistance genes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: YojI was found to be widely distributed among the major taxa comprising the BWWTP community such as the Comamonadaceae.
source: We further investigated which ARG subtypes contributed to the identified peptide resistance category and found that ~90% of the expressed peptide resistance was directly contributed by a single resistance gene, YojI, which was found to be widely distributed among the major taxa comprising the BWWTP community such as the Comamonadaceae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by detailed analysis of peptide resistance genes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: YojI is typically associated with resistance to microcins by reducing the intracellular concentration of the toxic antibiotic peptide.
source: YojI is typically associated with resistance to microcins by reducing the intracellular concentration of the toxic antibiotic peptide (Delgado et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Delgado et al., 2005.

claim: Taxa belonging to Acidimicrobiales, followed by Burkholderiales, were found to encode most of the ARGs.
source: Overall, taxa belonging to Acidimicrobiales, followed by Burkholderiales, were found to encode most of the ARGs (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic linkage of ARGs shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The abundance of ARGs linked to taxonomy varied over time.
source: Additionally, the abundance of ARGs linked to taxonomy varied over time.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal taxonomic linkage data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: During a five-week period (autumn: 02-11-2011 to 29-11-2011), a decrease in abundance in ARGs linked to Acidimicrobiales and Bacteroidales was observed coinciding with an increase in ARG abundance in Pseudomonadales and Lactobacillales.
source: This was most noticeable during a five-week period (autumn: 02-11-2011 to 29-11-2011), where a decrease in abundance in ARGs linked to Acidimicrobiales and Bacteroidales was observed coinciding with an increase in ARG abundance in Pseudomonadales and Lactobacillales.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal taxonomic linkage data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Candidatus Microthrix parvicella was identified as the main contributor to AMR within the order Acidimicrobiales.
source: Since the order Acidimicrobiales was found to be linked to the highest abundance in ARGs, we further resolved the taxonomic affiliation and identified the species Candidatus Microthrix parvicella (hereafter known as M. parvicella) to be the main contributor to AMR.
evidence: This is supported by taxonomic resolution of ARG contributors.

claim: M. parvicella was previously found to dominate this microbial community.
source: M. parvicella was previously found to dominate this microbial community (Martínez Arbas et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Martínez Arbas et al., 2021.

claim: M. parvicella is a well-characterized bacterium commonly occurring in the BWWTP.
source: and is a well-characterized bacterium commonly occurring in the BWWTP (Calusinska et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Calusinska et al., 2018.

claim: Aminoglycoside, beta-lactam, multidrug, and peptide resistance were found to be abundant in M. parvicella.
source: Overall, aminoglycoside, beta-lactam, multidrug, and peptide resistance were found to be abundant in this species (Figure 2b)

claim: Aminoglycoside resistance demonstrated the highest expression levels in M. parvicella as confirmed through metatranscriptomic analysis.
source: with aminoglycoside resistance demonstrating the highest expression levels as confirmed through metatranscriptomic analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: An almost complete decrease in ARGs was observed at two timepoints (23-11-2011 and 29-11-2011) coupled to a decrease in the abundance of M. parvicella itself.
source: Furthermore, coupled to a decrease in the abundance of M. parvicella itself (Martínez Arbas et al., 2021), we observed an almost complete decrease in ARGs at two timepoints (23-11-2011 and 29-11-2011).

claim: The M. parvicella population recovered to levels resembling the earlier timepoints in conjunction with the abundances in ARGs toward the end of the sampling period.
source: However, the M. parvicella population recovered to levels resembling the earlier timepoints in conjunction with the abundances in ARGs toward the end of the sampling period (Figure 2a, Figure 2b)

claim: ARGs, within or across ARG types and microbial taxa, showed clear and distinct co-occurrence patterns within the BWWTP.

claim: M. parvicella encoded different aminoglycoside resistance genes.

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa encoded and expressed the highest abundance of ARGs among identified pathogens over time within the BWWTP.

claim: Phages and plasmids contributed differentially to AMR.
